name: Currant Wine
description: Historical recipe from Miss Leslie's Complete Cookery (1851). Source method; not modernized or kitchen-tested.

ingredients.name: gallons and a half of water
ingredients.originalText: 2 gallons and a half of water

ingredients.name: and a half of the best loaf-sugar
ingredients.originalText: 5 pounds and a half of the best loaf-sugar

ingredients.name: cream of tartar
ingredients.originalText: half an ounce of cream of tartar

instructions.text: Strip the currants from the stalks into a great stone jar that has a cover to it, and mash them with a long thick stick
Then put the currants into a large linen bag; wash out the jar, set it under the bag, and squeeze the juice into it
Boil together two gallons and a half of water, and five pounds and a half of the best loaf-sugar, skimming it well
When the scum ceases to rise, mix the syrup with the currant juice
Let it stand a fortnight or three weeks to settle
Then transfer it to another vessel, taking care not to disturb the lees or dregs
If it is not quite clear and bright, refine it by mixing with a quart of the wine, (taken out for the purpose,) the whites of two eggs beaten to a stiff froth, and half an ounce of cream of tartar
Pour this gradually into the vessel
Let it stand ten days, and then bottle it off
Place the bottles in saw-dust, laying them on their sides
Take care that the saw-dust is not from pine wood

source.author: Eliza Leslie
source.originalInstructions:
1. Strip the currants from the stalks into a great stone jar that has a cover to it, and mash them with a long thick stick
2. Let them stand twenty-four hours
3. Then put the currants into a large linen bag; wash out the jar, set it under the bag, and squeeze the juice into it
4. Boil together two gallons and a half of water, and five pounds and a half of the best loaf-sugar, skimming it well
5. When the scum ceases to rise, mix the syrup with the currant juice
6. Let it stand a fortnight or three weeks to settle
7. Then transfer it to another vessel, taking care not to disturb the lees or dregs
8. If it is not quite clear and bright, refine it by mixing with a quart of the wine, (taken out for the purpose,) the whites of two eggs beaten to a stiff froth, and half an ounce of cream of tartar
9. Pour this gradually into the vessel
10. Let it stand ten days, and then bottle it off
11. Place the bottles in saw-dust, laying them on their sides
12. Take care that the saw-dust is not from pine wood
